items.prompt: In this unit, what does scope measure?
choices: How technically difficult your daily tasks tend to be
How many teams' decisions your judgment is expected to shape
Years of service
items.explanation: How many teams' decisions your judgment is expected to shape. Scope is the number of teams whose decisions your judgment shapes, and technical direction is the tool for it.

items.prompt: Technical direction means what?
choices: Steering others' decisions
Implementing every decision yourself, personally
Managing people through formal authority
items.explanation: Steering others' decisions. Scope is the number of teams whose decisions your judgment shapes, and technical direction is the tool for it.

items.prompt: Three teams each hand-rolled the same unsafe retry. How is that best described?

Not a problem
One pattern with one shared cause
items.explanation: One pattern with one shared cause. Scope is the number of teams whose decisions your judgment shapes, and technical direction is the tool for it.

Only the VP
items.explanation: Engineers on other teams. Scope is the number of teams whose decisions your judgment shapes, and technical direction is the tool for it.

items.prompt: What bounds purely individual execution?
choices: Your hours
The size of the company
The vendor's uptime guarantees
items.explanation: Your hours. Scope is the number of teams whose decisions your judgment shapes, and technical direction is the tool for it.

items.prompt: Does being the strongest engineer on your team automatically give you cross-team scope?
choices: Yes, skill converts directly
Yes, after a year
No, it is a different shape of ownership
items.explanation: No, it is a different shape of ownership. Scope is the number of teams whose decisions your judgment shapes, and technical direction is the tool for it.

items.prompt: Why does the retry bug call for more than one team's roadmap?
choices: It is technically harder than anything else
No single team's roadmap fixes it alone
Only one team uses the vendor
items.explanation: No single team's roadmap fixes it alone. Scope is the number of teams whose decisions your judgment shapes, and technical direction is the tool for it.

items.prompt: Is cross-team scope the same as managing people?
choices: No, it needs no reports
Yes, it requires direct reports
Yes, it needs a formal title first
items.explanation: No, it needs no reports. Scope is the number of teams whose decisions your judgment shapes, and technical direction is the tool for it.

items.prompt: Priya ships twice as much as anyone on her team, and her manager calls her ready for broader scope on that basis. Which reading fits this unit?
choices: Her output proves cross-team scope, since shipping at that rate necessarily shapes other teams' decisions
Broader scope comes with a title change, so her manager's call is the only evidence that matters
Team output is not cross-team scope; she must shape decisions on teams she is not on
Her output is too high, because scope is measured by how little code one person writes
items.explanation: Output on one's own team is measured within one roadmap. Cross-team scope means shaping decisions on teams she does not sit on, which shipping volume alone does not show.
items.reference:
Two shapes of ownership
own team: one roadmap, your hours, your code
across teams: several roadmaps, none fixes it alone
tool: technical direction, steering what others build
Why: scope counts how many teams' decisions your judgment shapes, not how hard your own work is.
items.learnMore:
Scope, not difficulty

Cross-team ownership is a different shape of work, not a harder version of team-level work. Being the best engineer in your group does not by itself produce it.

Common mistake

Reading scope as skill. A very skilled engineer can still have a team-sized scope.
items.reflection: Think of a problem you saw that several groups each solved separately. Whose job was it to notice the pattern?

items.prompt: Bug A is a flaky test in one team's pipeline. Bug B is a token-expiry mismatch that four teams each patched differently. Which one raises a cross-team ownership question?
choices: Bug B, because four roadmaps each hold a piece and none will close it alone
Bug A, because flaky tests are hard to diagnose
Both equally, because hard-to-reproduce bugs span every team
Neither, because a bug already patched by every team is no longer a problem
items.explanation: Bug B has four roadmaps each holding a piece and none able to close it alone. Bug A sits inside a single pipeline, so one team can own it.

items.prompt: Dana fixes a CSV-export quoting bug in a day. She notices two other teams copied her export code. What does leverage suggest as the next step?
choices: Check whether the copies share the cause, then offer one fix the others can adopt
Leave it, because her own team's fix is complete and the copies belong to the other teams to deal with
Rewrite both copies herself over the weekend so nobody else has to be asked
Announce in chat that the code is unsafe and let each team decide independently
items.explanation: Dana should first confirm the copies share the cause, then offer one fix others adopt. Rewriting them herself or only announcing the problem leaves the pattern open or spends her hours instead of multiplying them.
items.reference:
One bug, two reaches
Friday fix: Payments only, about a third of the $40,000
shared approach: all three teams, whole pattern closed
question: whose problem is this at my scope?

items.learnMore:
Correct is not the same as highest leverage

The Friday fix is good engineering. The question is whether it is the best use of the person who found the pattern, given who else is bleeding.

Common mistake

Treating every quick fix as a mistake. Narrow, urgent, ownerless problems still deserve the keyboard.

items.reference:
Three questions, in order
1. blast radius: how many teams or how much money?

Why: direction beats personal execution only when all three come back high.
items.learnMore:
Choosing a lever, not banning one

The three questions pick between fixing it yourself, coordinating several smaller fixes, and steering a shared one. A narrow, urgent, ownerless problem still gets the keyboard.

Common mistake

Applying direction to everything. For a narrow one-off it is slower than the fix, with no leverage gained.
